title: Nvidia's big bet on physical AI aims for safer robotaxis, humanoid robots
gist: Nvidia is betting billions on physical AI beyond data-center chips, and has extended its Halos safety stack from self-driving cars to robots via Halos for Robotics (June 2026). Nvidia's Amit Goel says safety is the next bottleneck for robots, and partners like Agility Robotics and Boston Dynamics are already adopting it, while Jensen Huang says physical AI already brings nearly $10 billion in annual revenue.

insights.claim: Jensen Huang said on the All-In Podcast in March 2026 that physical AI already drives nearly $10 billion in annual revenue for Nvidia, and he began calling it the company's second-most important growth category in 2025.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Robotics and autonomy is a sizable non-data-center revenue line that diversifies the Nvidia story.
insights.locator: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described the physical AI business

insights.claim: Nvidia has invested directly in robotics companies including Agility Robotics and Figure AI, plus robotics foundation model developers, and partnered with Chinese firm Unitree on an open humanoid robot reference design.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Nvidia is seeding the robotics ecosystem it wants to sell compute into, including a China-based partner.
insights.locator: The tech giant has also invested directly

insights.claim: Nvidia launched Halos in 2025 as hardware and software guardrails for autonomous vehicles and expanded it with Halos for Robotics in June 2026, targeting warehouse robots, factory humanoids and surgical robots.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Nvidia is productizing safety as a platform layer, potentially a switching-cost moat for robotics developers.

insights.claim: Amit Goel says that now that AI models and robot hardware are capable, safety is the next bottleneck, which is why Nvidia launched Halos for Robotics.
insights.speaker: Amit Goel
insights.so_what: Safety certification may gate commercial robot deployment more than raw capability does.
insights.quote: “Now the AI models are getting capable, the robot hardware is getting capable, and a thing we thought is going to be the next bottleneck is safety,”

insights.claim: The Halos stack combines the IGX Thor module with an independent safety processor, an operating system that monitors every hardware block and software library and isolates safety-critical workloads, a Holoscan Sensor Bridge to detect corrupted data, simulation, and an inspection lab program.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Nvidia is offering a vertically integrated safety stack, from silicon to inspection, which deepens lock-in to its platform.
insights.locator: Expanding safety from AVs to robots

insights.claim: Goel says functional and safety systems must run on the same silicon in physical AI.
insights.speaker: Amit Goel
insights.so_what: Consolidated silicon with a dedicated safety processor is Nvidia's hardware argument for its robotics computers.
insights.quote: “In the context of physical AI, you need to have your functional system and your safety system all running on the same silicon,”
insights.locator: Expanding safety from AVs to robots

themes.theme: Why robot safety is harder than AV safety

insights.claim: Functional safety for autonomous driving is generally consistent across automakers and countries, but a robot vacuum and a robotic forklift have very different safety needs, so Nvidia had to build a programmable platform that lets developers define custom safety functions.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Fragmented safety definitions make robotics standardization harder than in automotive.
insights.locator: However, adapting Nvidia Halos from autonomous vehicles

insights.claim: Goel notes that flexibility can come at the cost of losing control over the stack, the tradeoff Nvidia had to manage when letting developers customize safety.
insights.speaker: Amit Goel
insights.so_what: Customization versus integrity is the central design tension for a safety platform.
insights.quote: “Because giving flexibility can come at the cost of losing some control over the stack.”

insights.claim: Robots in unstructured environments like factories, warehouses and hospitals cannot see around corners, so a robot moving six miles per hour almost halts before a turn, limiting throughput without better safety.
insights.speaker: Amit Goel
insights.so_what: Better onboard safety translates directly into robot productivity and economics.
insights.locator: Custom safety functions are also necessary

insights.claim: Agility Robotics was first to incorporate Halos into its Digit 5 humanoid, bringing safety sensors on board so it needs no isolated workstations or external sensors around a work cell.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Moving safety on-robot lowers deployment cost and infrastructure friction for humanoids.
insights.quote: “Now the robot is literally unchained—the safety goes with the robot wherever it goes,”

insights.claim: Boston Dynamics is an early partner in the Halos safety accreditation program for Spot, Stretch and Atlas, with Atlas humanoids potentially deploying in parent Hyundai's automotive factories by 2028.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A 2028 Hyundai factory timeline sets a rough horizon for industrial humanoid scale.
insights.locator: The Massachusetts-based robotics company Boston Dynamics

insights.claim: KION Group is working to incorporate Halos for self-driving forklifts, and LG is developing a humanoid based on Nvidia's Isaac GROOT foundation model.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Industrial-logistics and consumer-electronics incumbents are adopting Nvidia's robotics stack.
insights.locator: Other companies working to incorporate Nvidia Halos

insights.claim: Hsu says it remains to be seen whether humanoids can become general-purpose workers, but the US, China and Europe are pushing robot deployment well beyond humanoids.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Humanoid generality is unproven, but broader robot adoption is a nearer-term driver for safety demand.
